newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech PM Klaus says stable crown policies continue.
newsitem.headline: Czech PM Klaus says stable crown policies continue.

text.p: Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, on Monday said his government remained committed to keeping the country's currency stable and interest rates high, boosting the crown to a 10-day high against its currency basket.
Speaking at the opening ceremony of an international engineering exhibition in the Czech second city of Brno, Klaus said a stable crown was a cornerstone of the country's economic restructuring.

"Together with the central bank, we are ready to continue in the policy of a stable exchange rate which gave our business sector so many stable points in the turbulent waters of liberalisation," Klaus said.

"In this phase, the policy of a stable exchange rate is a good tool, stimulating the restructuring of privatised companies, and it stimulates higher effectiveness and competitiveness on foreign markets."
Klaus, a monetarist economist, added that as a result of these policies, interest rates would remain high, at least over the short-term.
"The best way to face this problem is a decline in inflation, and ... an improvement of cautiousness of commercial banks and through that a decrease in the share of risky loans," he said.
"(But) a short-term solution of this important problem (high interest rates) doesn't exist," Klaus added.
Klaus also said that better supervision of banks by the central bank would help the Czech credit environment.
Czech inflation has been one of the lowest in the region, but after dropping below double digits last year, it has remained stubbornly high at around nine percent annually.
In August the monthly rate was only 0.2 percent, but the year-on-year figure rose to 9.6 percent, putting government forcasts of eight percent in flation by year's end seriously in doubt.
The central bank discount rate currently stands at 10.5 percent, while its last resort lending facility for banks, the Lombard rate, stands at 14 percent.

The forex market reacted swiftly to the PM's comments, strengthening immediately by some 30 basis points against the dollar to a 10-day high against its fixing basket of around +4.3 percent before profit-taking set in, taking back much of the gain.

"The advantage of high interest rates will at least remain the same for the short-term, which definitely gives a signal to the market, but there is still a question as to whether it will give the crown a long-term boost," said Petr Korous, a dealer at Ceskoslovenska Obchodni Banka.
"But the market is so liquid that we can't expect to see the crown strengthen continually without profit-taking, which we saw occur," he added.

The crown is fixed daily at within a plus or minus 7.5 percent of the mark/dollar basket midpoint. On Monday, it was fixed at 26.465 to the dollar, implying a deviation from the mark/dollar basket midpoint of plus 4.15 percent.
In his speech Klaus also said that the country's abnormally low unemployment level, stuck at around three percent, has kept the labour pool weak and the ensuing wage pressure was inflationary.
"We consider the problems caused by the insufficient pool of labour as serious," he said.
The PM also said that the country's ballooning current account deficit was still financeable, though his government was watching its development closely.
